lessons.title: Printing and paging through files
lessons.summary: Look inside a text file without opening an editor.

blocks.text: Most files you'll meet are plain text: README files, FASTA sequences, PDB structures, logs, scores. You can read them right in the terminal.

command.name: cat
command.what: Prints the whole file. Give it several files and it prints them one after another, which is where the name comes from. Best for short files.

command.name: less
command.what: Shows a long file one screen at a time. Space or arrow keys move, `/word` searches, `q` quits. Use it for logs and structures too long for cat.

blocks.tip: `cat -n` numbers the lines. Useful when an error message says "line 37".

quiz.q: A log file is 50,000 lines long. What's the best way to look through it?
options: Open it in a word processor
quiz.why: cat would scroll 50,000 lines past you. less lets you page and search.

lessons.title: The start and the end: head and tail
lessons.summary: Often you only need the first or last few lines.

command.name: head
command.what: Prints the first 10 lines, or the first N with `-n N`. Good for headers: the top of a PDB or a CSV.

flags: Keep printing new lines as a running job writes them; Ctrl+C stops

lessons.title: Finding lines with grep
lessons.summary: Pull out just the lines you care about, or count them.

command.name: grep
command.what: Prints only the lines that contain TEXT. Put TEXT in quotes if it has spaces or symbols like > or *.

flags: Print how many lines match instead of the lines
Print lines that do NOT match

blocks.text: In a FASTA file, every sequence starts with a header line beginning with `>`. Counting those lines counts the sequences.

blocks.warn: `grep > file` without quotes doesn't search for >. The shell sees > as "send output to file" and overwrites the file. Always quote it: `grep ">" file`.

quiz.q: Which counts the lines in `log.txt` that do NOT contain `ok`?
quiz.why: -v flips the match to lines without ok, and -c counts them. Letters combine, so -vc is -v -c.

lessons.title: Columns, sorting and pipes
lessons.summary: Rank designs by a score column, and chain commands together.

blocks.text: Score files are tables: one row per design, columns separated by spaces or commas. Three commands work on columns: `sort` puts rows in order, `cut` keeps only some columns, and `head` or `tail` picks the top or bottom.

command.name: sort
command.what: Sorts lines alphabetically, or by number with -n. -k picks which column to sort by.

flags: Compare as numbers, so 10 comes after 9 (not after 1)

try.text: Sort `scores.txt` by its second column, lowest (best) score first.

command.name: cut
command.what: Keeps only the columns (fields) you list. `cut -d , -f 1,3 summary.csv` prints the name and ipTM columns.

quiz.why: Without -n, sort compares text character by character. -n compares the values as numbers.

lessons.title: Comparing two files
lessons.summary: Spot exactly what changed between two versions.

command.name: diff
command.what: Prints only the lines that differ. Lines from the first file start with `<`, lines from the second with `>`. No output means the files are identical.

example.note: `2c2` means line 2 changed. The old value is above the dashes, the new one below.

try.text: What changed between the two configs?
